newsitem.title: HAITI: Crowds protest after gangsters kill six in Haiti.
newsitem.headline: Crowds protest after gangsters kill six in Haiti.

text.p: Crowds burned piles of rubber tires in the streets of a town outside the Haitian capital on Friday in a protest after gangsters killed up to six residents in a nighttime shooting spree.

Black smoke billowed in the air as hundreds of people milled around in the main intersection of Croix de Bouquet. A corpse was burning among the tires and residents said it was that of a thief killed by vigilantes in retaliation for Thursday night's shootings.

"There was a vehicle which came through town last night," United Nations police trainer Gherdy Francis of the United States said at the scene. "They drove around shooting and now people are showing their disapproval."

He said three people were killed and three wounded on Thursday night but a Haitian police officer said he had seen six bodies. Witnesses said the gangsters drove through town at about 9 p.m. (0200 GMT on Friday) asking for members of a neighbourhood watch group.

One victim, Herald Rene, worked as a courthouse security guard. The gunmen, numbering about a dozen, wore masks and were piled aboard a white Toyota pickup, the witnesses said. They were armed with 9 mm pistols.
By late afternoon police had arrested five suspects, according to Radio Metropole. It gave no further details.
President Rene Preval visited the area in a show of support.
"We need to reinforce protection for the people. We are here to have a dialogue with them," he told reporters.

U.N. officials said the violence was part of a power struggle in the town between outlaws and various competing security forces. "We have had serious problems of vigilantism in the area," one official said.

There has also been a recent conflict between the town's mayor, who has his own security force, and the local Haitian National Police, he said. "When the HNP arrested one of the members of the mayor's security team, the mayor's office threatened to attack the HNP," he said.
"Whatever happened today, there is certainly trouble brewing."
Such conflicts have arisen in cities throughout Haiti as mayors recruit their own security forces.

About 1,300 U.N. troops have been patrolling Haiti in a peacekeeping mission to support the new Haitian police force. But the force, created about a year ago by foreign police trainers, is not yet able to guarantee law and order.
Demoralised trainers in Croix de Bouquet told Reuters recently there was little hope for the new force, formed to replace a repressive military disbanded in 1995.
"When the U.N. leaves, the police are going to become what the military was," one said. He said prisoners had been murdered and beaten with rocks by the local police.
The lack of security has led to vigilantism. U.N. officials said criminals in increasing numbers had been burned and hacked with machetes.
